turns.doctor_question: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming today. What brings you in to see me?
turns.patient_response:
Hi. Thanks. Well, I came in because I just can't stop focusing on my face. Specifically, the left side of my face looks really uneven and puffy to me. I notice it constantly, especially on video calls for work and in photos from my salsa classes. 

Everyone keeps telling me they don't see anything at all, but I just can't unsee it. It's getting to the point where it's really starting to mess with my job and my social life, so I figured I needed to talk to someone about it.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient reports being persistently preoccupied with a perceived flaw in their face (unevenness and puffiness on the left side) that others state they cannot see.

turns.doctor_question: Do you find yourself doing things like checking mirrors repeatedly, trying to cover or camouflage that side of your face, or comparing your face to other people's throughout the day?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, definitely. Before my work meetings or if I'm getting ready to go out, I just keep opening the camera preview. I'll spend a lot of time changing the angle and adjusting the lighting, and... fixing my hair so it falls around that side of my face to try and hide it. 

If I'm taking pictures, I end up retaking them over and over again. I also ask my friends constantly if I look strange. It gets to the point where I do all this until I'm either running late, or honestly, I just feel too drained to even go out at all.

symptom_reasoning.S068: The patient confirms engaging in repetitive behaviors to address appearance concerns, including repeatedly checking camera previews, camouflaging their face with their hair, retaking photos, and constantly seeking reassurance from friends.

turns.doctor_question: When your friends or coworkers tell you they don't notice any unevenness, do you think it's possible they're right and your face actually looks normal, or do you feel convinced that the flaw is really there no matter what they say?
turns.patient_response: I mean, I hear them when they say that, and part of me knows they aren't lying to me. But... when I look in the mirror or at a photo, I just see it so clearly. So, even though they say it's fine, I still feel completely convinced that it's there and that everyone can see it. It's really hard to believe them when my own eyes are telling me something else.
